decks.title: Some Applications of Trigonometry — Part 1: Elevation, depression and one triangle
goals: Identify the line of sight and the angles of elevation and depression in a described situation
Draw and label the figure for a heights-and-distances problem
Explain why an angle of depression equals the corresponding angle of elevation
Find a height, a distance or a slant length using one right triangle
Allow for the observer’s eye height

slides.heading: Some Applications of Trigonometry, Part 1: Looking up and looking down
slides.body_md: How tall is a tower you cannot climb? Measure one distance and one angle.

visual.alt: A tower BT seen from a point O on level ground 50 metres from its foot B; the line of sight OT makes an angle of elevation of 45 degrees with the ground, and the tower height is unknown. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: At $45^\circ$ the height equals the distance (drawn to scale).

slides.narration: Welcome. Surveyors find the heights of towers, temples and hills without ever climbing them. They stand at a known distance, measure the angle up to the top, and let trigonometry do the rest. Here, from fifty metres away, the top is at forty five degrees, so the tower is fifty metres tall. In this part you will learn to set up such problems correctly.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Identify the **line of sight**, the **angle of elevation** and the **angle of depression**
Draw and label the figure from a description
Explain why depression at the top equals elevation at the bottom
Find heights, distances and slant lengths with one right triangle
Allow for eye height
slides.narration: These are your goals. The syllabus limits problems to at most two right triangles and to angles of thirty, forty five and sixty degrees, so the trigonometry is always exact. The real skill is the figure: if the drawing is right, the calculation is usually one line.

slides.heading: The angle of elevation
slides.body_md: The **line of sight** joins the observer’s eye to the object. If the object is **above** the horizontal through the eye, the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight is the **angle of elevation**.

visual.alt: An observer O looks up at the top T of an object BT; the angle between the horizontal OB and the line of sight OT is the angle of elevation, here 30 degrees, with a right angle at B.
visual.caption: Angle of elevation: from the horizontal **up** to the line of sight.

slides.narration: Imagine looking straight ahead, parallel to the ground. That is your horizontal. To see the top of a tower you raise your eyes. The angle you turn through, from the horizontal up to the line of sight, is the angle of elevation. It is measured at the observer, never at the object.

slides.heading: The angle of depression
slides.body_md: If the object is **below** the horizontal through the eye, the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight is the **angle of depression**.

visual.alt: An observer at the top T of a cliff BT looks down at a boat P; the angle between the dashed horizontal through T and the line of sight TP is the angle of depression, 30 degrees.
visual.caption: Angle of depression: from the horizontal **down** to the line of sight.

slides.narration: Now stand on a cliff and look down at a boat. Again start from the horizontal through your eye, drawn dashed here, and turn down to the line of sight. That angle is the angle of depression. A common error is to measure it from the vertical cliff instead. The horizontal is always the starting line.

slides.heading: Depression equals elevation
slides.body_md: The horizontal at the top is parallel to the ground. The line of sight cuts both, so the angle of depression at $T$ and the angle of elevation at $P$ are **alternate angles**, and they are equal.

visual.alt: From the top T of a tower BT, the angle of depression of P is 40 degrees; at P the angle of elevation of T is also 40 degrees. The dashed horizontal at T is parallel to the ground, and the two equal angles are alternate angles.
visual.caption: Depression at $T$ $=$ elevation at $P$ (alternate angles).

slides.narration: Here is the key fact for depression problems. The dashed horizontal at the top and the ground are parallel lines, and the line of sight crosses them. Alternate angles are equal, so the forty degree angle of depression at the top reappears as a forty degree angle of elevation at the bottom. You can then work inside the right triangle.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from a balcony
slides.body_md: From a balcony $12$ m above a road in Mumbai, Meena sees a car at an angle of depression of $30^\circ$. Draw the figure and find the distance of the car from the foot of the building.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Draw the vertical $BW = 12$ m, the road $BC$, the dashed horizontal at $W$; mark $30^\circ$ below it.
**Step 2 —** By alternate angles, $\angle WCB = 30^\circ$; the right angle is at $B$.
**Step 3 —** $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{12}{BC} \Rightarrow BC = 12\sqrt3 \approx 20.78$ m.
**Check —** The car is farther away than the balcony is high, as a small angle suggests ✓.

visual.alt: A balcony W 12 metres above the road at B; a car C on the road is seen at an angle of depression of 30 degrees, and the angle of elevation of W from the car is also 30 degrees. The distance BC is unknown. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: Use the equal angle at $C$: $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{12}{BC}$.

slides.narration: Always draw first. Put the vertical building, the road, and the dashed horizontal at the balcony. Mark the angle of depression from that horizontal. Then move the same angle down to the car using alternate angles. Now the triangle has the right angle at the foot, and tangent links the height with the distance.

slides.heading: Quick check: equal angles
slides.body_md: Which two angles are alternate angles?
slides.narration: Picture the horizontal at the top and the sea surface. The line of sight crosses both. Which angle at the boat matches the angle at the top?

slides.heading: A method for every problem
slides.body_md: Draw, mark, label, then choose the ratio that links the known side and the unknown side.

nodes.label: Draw the figure: verticals, ground, eye level
Mark the angle at the observer and the right angle
Label the known length and the unknown

visual.alt: Method chart: draw the figure with verticals, ground and eye level; mark the angle at the observer and the right angle; label the known length and the unknown; choose tangent for opposite and adjacent, sine for opposite and hypotenuse, cosine for adjacent and hypotenuse; then solve, rationalise and approximate using root 3 approximately 1.732.
visual.caption: Most height-and-distance problems need $\tan$.

slides.narration: Every heights and distances problem follows the same plan. Draw the verticals, the ground and the eye level. Mark the angle at the observer and the right angle. Label what you know and what you want. Then choose the ratio: tangent if the two sides are the height and the ground distance, sine or cosine if the slant line is involved.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: height of a gopuram
slides.body_md: From a point $40$ m from the foot of a temple gopuram in Madurai, the angle of elevation of its top is $60^\circ$. Find its height.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Right angle at the foot $B$; known: $OB = 40$ m; wanted: $h = BT$.
**Step 2 —** Opposite and adjacent: $\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{40}$.
**Step 3 —** $h = 40\sqrt3 \approx 40 \times 1.732 = 69.28$ m.
**Check —** At $60^\circ$ the height should exceed the distance: $69.28 > 40$ ✓.

visual.alt: A temple gopuram BT seen from O, 40 metres from its foot B, at an angle of elevation of 60 degrees; the height h is unknown. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: $\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{40}$.

slides.narration: The two sides involved are the height and the ground distance, so the ratio is tangent. Sixty degrees gives root three. Multiply, and approximate only at the very end using one point seven three two. A quick sense check helps: a steep angle means a tall object compared with your distance.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a slant length
slides.body_md: A drone hovers $45$ m above a Holi ground. Its tether, pulled straight, makes $30^\circ$ with the ground. How long is the tether?
bullets: **Step 1 —** Known: height $45$ m (opposite the $30^\circ$ angle). Wanted: the tether (hypotenuse).
**Step 2 —** $\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{45}{l}$.
**Contrast —** Using $\tan 30^\circ$ would give the ground distance, $45\sqrt3 \approx 77.94$ m, not the tether.

visual.alt: A drone T hovering 45 metres above the point B; its tether from O on the ground makes 30 degrees with the ground; the tether length OT is unknown. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: Height and hypotenuse: use $\sin 30^\circ$.

slides.narration: This time the unknown is the slant line, the hypotenuse. Opposite and hypotenuse means sine. Sine thirty degrees is one half, so the tether is twice the height. If you had used tangent, you would have found the ground distance instead, a different length. Always name the two sides before choosing a ratio.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a boat from a cliff
slides.body_md: From the top of a $50$ m cliff at Varkala, the angle of depression of a boat is $30^\circ$. How far is the boat from the foot of the cliff?
bullets: **Step 1 —** Alternate angles: the angle of elevation of the cliff top from the boat is $30^\circ$.
**Step 2 —** $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{50}{BP}$.
**Step 3 —** $BP = 50\sqrt3 \approx 86.6$ m.
**Check —** $\dfrac{50}{86.6} \approx 0.577 = \tan 30^\circ$ ✓.

visual.alt: A cliff BT 50 metres high; a boat P is seen from the top at an angle of depression of 30 degrees; the distance BP is unknown. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{50}{BP}$.

slides.narration: Transfer the angle of depression to the boat using alternate angles. Now the boat sees the cliff top at thirty degrees, and tangent links the cliff height with the distance. Dividing by tangent thirty is the same as multiplying by root three. The check divides the height by your distance and compares it with tangent thirty.

slides.heading: Quick check: a depression problem
slides.body_md: Move the angle to the scooter first.
slides.narration: The angle of depression at the top equals the angle of elevation at the scooter. Which ratio links the height and the distance?

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a ladder
slides.body_md: An $8$ m ladder leans against a wall in a Pune housing society, making $60^\circ$ with the ground. How high does it reach, and how far is its foot from the wall?
bullets: **Step 1 —** The ladder is the hypotenuse, $8$ m.
**Step 2 —** Height: $\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{8} \Rightarrow h = 4\sqrt3 \approx 6.93$ m.
**Step 3 —** Foot: $\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{d}{8} \Rightarrow d = 4$ m.

visual.alt: A ladder OT, 8 metres long, leaning against a wall BT and making 60 degrees with the ground; the foot distance OB and the height BT are unknown. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: Hypotenuse known: $\sin$ gives the height, $\cos$ gives the foot distance.

slides.narration: With the hypotenuse known, sine gives the side opposite the angle, the height, and cosine gives the adjacent side, the distance of the foot. Pythagoras makes a perfect check: the two answers squared must add up to the ladder squared.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: allow for eye height
slides.body_md: A student whose eyes are $1.6$ m above the ground sees the top of a $21.6$ m flagpole at an angle of elevation of $45^\circ$. How far is she from the pole?
bullets: **Step 1 —** The angle is measured at her **eye**: the horizontal from $E$ meets the pole at $M$, $1.6$ m up.
**Step 3 —** $\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{20}{EM} \Rightarrow EM = 20$ m. She is $20$ m from the pole.
**Contrast —** Ignoring eye height would give $21.6$ m, an error of $1.6$ m.

visual.alt: A student with eye E 1.6 metres above the ground looks at the top T of a 21.6 metre flagpole BT; the dashed horizontal from E meets the pole at M; the angle of elevation at E is 45 degrees; her distance is unknown. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: Only $21.6 - 1.6 = 20$ m of the pole is above eye level.

slides.narration: Angles are measured at the eye, not at the feet. So draw the horizontal from the eye to the pole. The right triangle sits above that line, and only twenty metres of the pole are in it. When a question gives the observer’s height, it is there for a reason: subtract it first.

slides.heading: Quick check: eye height
slides.body_md: Subtract or add the eye height?
slides.narration: Find the height above eye level from the angle and distance. Then decide: should the eye height be added or subtracted to get the full tower?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Angles of elevation and depression are measured from the **horizontal through the eye**
Depression at the top $=$ elevation at the bottom (alternate angles)
Draw, mark the right angle, label known and unknown
$\tan$ for height and distance; $\sin$/$\cos$ when a slant length is involved
Subtract eye height before using the triangle

visual.alt: Table: from a distance to a height, or a height to a distance, use tangent; from a height to a slant length use sine; from a slant length to a distance use cosine; with an example of each.
visual.caption: Pick the ratio from the two sides involved.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. Both angles start from the horizontal through the eye. A depression at the top becomes an equal elevation at the bottom. Draw carefully, choose the ratio from the two sides involved, and allow for eye height. Then the arithmetic is short.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Figure (1 mark):** correct figure with the angle at the observer and the right angle marked
**Ratio (1 mark):** correct ratio with values substituted
**Answer (1 mark):** simplified exact form, then the approximate value with units
**Mistake:** angle of depression measured from the vertical
**Mistake:** $\sin$ instead of $\tan$ for height and distance
**Mistake:** eye height ignored
slides.narration: Examiners award a mark for a correct figure, so always draw one, even if the question does not ask. Then write the ratio with the numbers substituted, and finally give the exact answer and its decimal value with units. The three classic slips are measuring from the vertical, choosing the wrong ratio and forgetting the eye height.

decks.title: Some Applications of Trigonometry — Part 2: Problems with two right triangles
goals: Solve problems with two observation points on the same side of an object
Solve problems with observers on opposite sides
Solve problems with an object on top of another
Solve depression problems with two objects, and two-building problems
Find speeds of moving objects from changing angles

slides.heading: Some Applications of Trigonometry, Part 2: Two triangles, one answer
slides.body_md: One angle gives one equation. When the distance is unknown, a second angle gives the second equation.

visual.alt: A tower BT with two observation points C and D on the same side, 40 metres apart; the angle of elevation of T is 30 degrees from the farther point C and 60 degrees from the nearer point D. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: Two right triangles share the height $h$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Often you cannot reach the foot of a tower to measure your distance from it. The solution is to measure the angle of elevation from two points a known distance apart. That creates two right triangles sharing the same height, and two equations to solve. This part is all about such pairs.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Two points on the **same side**
Two observers on **opposite sides**
An object **on top of** another
Two objects seen **from a height**; two buildings
Speeds from **changing angles**
slides.narration: These are your goals: five common situations, each with exactly two right triangles. Spotting which situation you are in, and which side the two triangles share, is half the work.

slides.heading: Strategy for two triangles
slides.body_md: Find what the two triangles share (usually the height), then write one equation from each.

nodes.label: Find the side the two triangles share
Write one equation from each triangle

visual.alt: Strategy chart for two triangles: find the shared side, write one equation from each triangle, express the same unknown twice, equate or subtract and solve, then check both angles.
visual.caption: Two triangles, one shared side, two equations.

slides.narration: Here is the plan. First, find the side the two triangles have in common, usually the height of the tower. Next, write one tangent equation from each triangle. Then express one unknown in two ways and set them equal, or subtract. Finally, check that both angles really come out right.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: two points on the same side
slides.body_md: From two points $C$ and $D$, $40$ m apart on the same side of a tower, the angles of elevation of its top are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. Find its height.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Let $DB = x$, $BT = h$. Triangle $DBT$: $\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x} \Rightarrow h = x\sqrt3$.
**Step 2 —** Triangle $CBT$: $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x + 40} \Rightarrow x + 40 = h\sqrt3 = 3x \Rightarrow x = 20$.
**Step 3 —** $h = 20\sqrt3 \approx 34.64$ m.
**Check —** From $C$: $\dfrac{34.64}{60} \approx 0.577 = \tan 30^\circ$ ✓.

visual.alt: A balcony W 12 metres above the road at B; a car C on the road is seen at an angle of depression of 30 degrees, and the angle of elevation of W from the car is also 30 degrees. The distance BC is unknown. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: Use the equal angle at $C$: $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{12}{BC}$.

slides.narration: Both triangles contain the tower, so the height is shared. Write the nearer triangle first: it gives h in terms of x. Substitute into the farther triangle, and x comes out as twenty. Then the height follows. Check with the farther point: sixty metres away, the tangent should be one over root three.

slides.heading: The thirty–sixty pair
slides.body_md: With $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ from the same side, the gap between the points is $\dfrac{2h}{\sqrt3}$, and triangle $CDT$ is isosceles ($CD = DT$).

visual.alt: Table for the 30 and 60 degree pair: the nearer point is h over root 3 from the foot, the farther point is h root 3 away, so the gap is 2 h over root 3.
visual.caption: For the $30^\circ$–$60^\circ$ pair, the gap equals $\dfrac{2h}{\sqrt3}$; also $CD = DT$.

slides.narration: This pair appears so often that it is worth knowing its shape. The nearer point is h over root three from the foot and the farther point is h root three away. Their gap is two h over root three. Also, the angle at the top between the two lines of sight is thirty degrees, so the gap equals the nearer line of sight.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: opposite sides
slides.body_md: Two people stand on opposite sides of a tower in Hyderabad, $100$ m apart and in line with its foot. They see the top at $30^\circ$ and $45^\circ$. Find the height.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Distances: $h\sqrt3$ (at $30^\circ$) and $h$ (at $45^\circ$).
**Step 2 —** Opposite sides, so **add**: $h\sqrt3 + h = 100 \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt3 + 1}$.
**Step 3 —** Rationalise: $h = \dfrac{100(\sqrt3 - 1)}{2} = 50(\sqrt3 - 1) \approx 36.6$ m.

visual.alt: A tower BT between two observers P and Q on opposite sides, 100 metres apart; the angle of elevation of T is 30 degrees from P and 45 degrees from Q. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: $PB + BQ = h\sqrt3 + h = 100$ m.

slides.narration: When the observers are on opposite sides, their distances from the foot add up to the gap between them. Express both distances in terms of h and add. To simplify one over root three plus one, multiply top and bottom by root three minus one. Compare this with the same-side case, where the distances are subtracted.

slides.heading: Quick check: same side
slides.body_md: Two tangent equations, then subtract.
slides.narration: Express both distances from the foot in terms of the height. Their difference is the gap between the points. Solve for the height.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: an object on top
slides.body_md: A water tank stands on a $12$ m tower. From a point $P$ on the ground, the bottom of the tank is seen at $45^\circ$ and the top at $60^\circ$. Find the height of the tank.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Bottom at $45^\circ$: $PB = 12$ m.
**Step 2 —** Top at $60^\circ$: height of the top $= 12\tan 60^\circ = 12\sqrt3$ m.
**Step 3 —** Tank $= 12\sqrt3 - 12 = 12(\sqrt3 - 1) \approx 8.78$ m.
**Check —** $\dfrac{20.78}{12} \approx 1.73 = \tan 60^\circ$ ✓.

visual.alt: A 12 metre tower BT carrying a water tank TU; from a point P on the ground, the bottom T of the tank is seen at 45 degrees and the top U at 60 degrees. The tank height is unknown. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: Two angles at $P$ share the base $PB$.

slides.narration: Here both triangles share the base, the distance from P to the foot. The lower angle and the known tower height give that distance. The upper angle then gives the height of the top of the tank. The tank itself is the difference between the two heights.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: two cars from a tower
slides.body_md: From the top of a $60$ m tower beside the Mumbai–Pune expressway, the angles of depression of two cars on the same side are $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$. Find the distance between the cars.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Nearer car ($60^\circ$): $BP = \dfrac{60}{\sqrt3} = 20\sqrt3$ m.
**Step 2 —** Farther car ($30^\circ$): $BQ = 60\sqrt3$ m.
**Step 3 —** $PQ = 60\sqrt3 - 20\sqrt3 = 40\sqrt3 \approx 69.28$ m.
**Check —** The larger angle of depression belongs to the nearer car ✓.

visual.alt: From the top T of a 60 metre tower, two cars P and Q on a straight road on the same side are seen at angles of depression of 60 degrees and 30 degrees, measured from the dashed horizontal at T. The gap PQ is unknown. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: Find $BP$ and $BQ$, then subtract.

slides.narration: Each angle of depression moves down to its car by alternate angles, giving two triangles that share the tower. The steeper line of sight, sixty degrees, goes to the nearer car. Find each distance from the foot and subtract, because the cars are on the same side.

slides.heading: Five checks before you finish
slides.body_md: Most lost marks come from the figure, not the arithmetic.

rows: Depression angle marked at the object, measured from the vertical
measure from the horizontal through the observer
$\sin$ used when height and ground distance are involved
subtract it from the object height first
Same-side and opposite-side cases mixed up
same side: subtract distances; opposite: add

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes: measuring depression from the vertical instead of the horizontal; using sine where tangent is needed; ignoring eye height; mixing up same-side and opposite-side cases; and poor approximation of h over root 3.
visual.caption: Check these five before you finish.

slides.narration: Before you write your final answer, run through this list. Is every angle measured from the horizontal at the observer? Did you use tangent for height and ground distance? Did you allow for eye height? Did you add for opposite sides and subtract for the same side? And is your approximation done at the end, with root three as one point seven three two?

slides.heading: Worked example 5: two buildings
slides.body_md: Two buildings in Kolkata are $30$ m apart. From the foot of the shorter one, the top of the taller is seen at $60^\circ$; from the top of the shorter, at $30^\circ$. Find both heights.
bullets: **Step 1 —** From the foot: $H = 30\tan 60^\circ = 30\sqrt3 \approx 51.96$ m.
**Step 2 —** From the top (along the horizontal $AN$): $H - h = 30\tan 30^\circ = 10\sqrt3$.
**Step 3 —** $h = 30\sqrt3 - 10\sqrt3 = 20\sqrt3 \approx 34.64$ m.
**Check —** $\dfrac{H - h}{30} = \dfrac{10\sqrt3}{30} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ ✓.

visual.alt: Two buildings 30 metres apart: the shorter AP of height h and the taller RQ of height H. From the foot P, the top Q is seen at 60 degrees; from the top A, along the dashed horizontal AN, the top Q is seen at 30 degrees. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: From the foot: $H = 30\tan 60^\circ$. From the top: $H - h = 30\tan 30^\circ$.

slides.narration: Draw a dashed horizontal from the top of the shorter building to the taller one. It cuts the taller building into two parts: the part below, equal to the shorter building, and the part above. One triangle from the foot gives the whole height; the other, from the top, gives only the part above the horizontal.

slides.heading: Quick check: two shadows
slides.body_md: Shadow at each angle, then the difference.
slides.narration: Write each shadow as the height divided by the tangent of the angle. Their difference is given. Solve for the height.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a moving drone
slides.body_md: A drone flies horizontally at a steady $8$ m/s. From a point $O$, its angle of elevation is $60^\circ$; $10$ s later it is $30^\circ$. Find its height.
bullets: **Step 1 —** In $10$ s it covers $80$ m: $D_1D_2 = 80$ m.
**Step 2 —** Horizontal distances from $O$: $\dfrac{h}{\sqrt3}$ and $h\sqrt3$, so $h\sqrt3 - \dfrac{h}{\sqrt3} = 80$.
**Step 3 —** $\dfrac{2h}{\sqrt3} = 80 \Rightarrow h = 40\sqrt3 \approx 69.28$ m.
**Check —** Distances $40$ m and $120$ m; $\dfrac{69.28}{40} \approx 1.73$ and $\dfrac{69.28}{120} \approx 0.577$ ✓.

visual.alt: A drone flying horizontally at height h from position D1, seen from O at an angle of elevation of 60 degrees, to position D2, seen at 30 degrees, 80 metres further along. Drawn to scale.
visual.caption: Same height, two distances: $h\sqrt3 - \dfrac{h}{\sqrt3} = 80$.

slides.narration: A moving object at a fixed height gives two triangles with the same height. Speed times time gives the distance between the two positions. Write both horizontal distances in terms of the height, subtract, and solve. This is the thirty sixty pair again, so the gap is two h over root three.

slides.heading: Quick check: angles do not scale
slides.body_md: Does doubling the distance halve the angle?
slides.narration: Doubling the distance halves the tangent of the angle. Does it halve the angle itself? Try it with the values you know.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Find the shared side; write one equation per triangle
Same side: subtract distances; opposite sides: add
Object on top: shared base, two heights
Two buildings: split the taller one with a horizontal
Moving objects: distance $=$ speed $\times$ time between two positions

visual.alt: Table for the 30 and 60 degree pair: the nearer point is h over root 3 from the foot, the farther point is h root 3 away, so the gap is 2 h over root 3.
visual.caption: For the $30^\circ$–$60^\circ$ pair, the gap equals $\dfrac{2h}{\sqrt3}$; also $CD = DT$.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. Every problem here has two right triangles with one side in common. Write an equation for each, and combine them by adding, subtracting or substituting. Check each answer against both angles. With practice, you will recognise the situation from the first sentence.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Figure (1 mark):** both triangles, both angles at the right vertices, right angles marked
**Equations (1–2 marks):** one correct ratio equation per triangle
**Solving (1 mark):** eliminating the unknown, rationalising
**Answer (1 mark):** exact and approximate values with units
**Mistake:** adding distances for points on the same side
**Mistake:** marking the angle of depression at the object from the vertical
slides.narration: Long questions in this chapter carry four or five marks, and the figure alone is worth one. Write each ratio equation on its own line, then show the elimination. Rationalise before approximating, and give units. Above all, decide early whether the points are on the same side or opposite sides.

notes.title: Some Applications of Trigonometry — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Line of sight and angle of elevation
sections.body_md:
The **line of sight** is the line from the observer's eye to the object. The **horizontal** through the eye is the reference line for every angle in this chapter.

If the object is above the horizontal, the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight is the **angle of elevation**. It is measured **at the observer**. As the observer walks towards the object, the angle of elevation increases.

All problems use angles of $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ and at most two right triangles; exact answers use surds, and decimal answers use $\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$, $\sqrt2 \approx 1.414$.

key_terms.definition_md: The line from the observer’s eye to the object viewed.
The angle from the horizontal up to the line of sight, for an object above eye level.

visual.alt: An observer O looks up at the top T of an object BT; the angle between the horizontal OB and the line of sight OT is the angle of elevation, here 30 degrees, with a right angle at B.
visual.caption: Angle of elevation: from the horizontal **up** to the line of sight.

sections.heading: 2. Angle of depression; equal alternate angles
sections.body_md:
If the object is below the horizontal through the eye, the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight is the **angle of depression**. Draw the horizontal through the observer (dashed) and measure **down** from it — never from the vertical.

The horizontal at the top and the ground are parallel, and the line of sight is a transversal, so

$$\text{angle of depression of } P \text{ from } T = \text{angle of elevation of } T \text{ from } P \quad \text{(alternate angles)}.$$

Use this to move the angle into the right triangle at ground level.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle from the horizontal down to the line of sight, for an object below eye level.

sections.heading: 3. Problems with one right triangle
sections.body_md:
**Method:** draw the figure → mark the angle at the observer and the right angle → label the known side and the unknown → choose the ratio → solve, rationalise, approximate.

- Height and ground distance: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}}$. A gopuram seen at $60^\circ$ from $40$ m: $h = 40\sqrt3 \approx 69.28$ m.
- Height and slant line: $\sin\theta$. A tether at $30^\circ$ holding a drone $45$ m up is $90$ m long.
- Slant line and ground distance: $\cos\theta$. An $8$ m ladder at $60^\circ$ has its foot $4$ m out.
- Shadows: shadow $= \dfrac{h}{\tan\theta}$; at $45^\circ$ the shadow equals the height; higher sun, shorter shadow.

key_terms.definition_md: The sun’s elevation is the angle at the tip of the shadow; shadow length $= \dfrac{h}{\tan\theta}$.

sections.heading: 4. Eye height and objects at different levels
sections.body_md:
Angles are measured at the **eye**. If the observer's eyes are $e$ m above the ground, draw the horizontal from the eye; only the part of the object above it, $h - e$, belongs to the right triangle.

Example: eyes at $1.6$ m, a $21.6$ m flagpole at $45^\circ$: $21.6 - 1.6 = 20$, so the distance is $20$ m. Likewise, an observer on a deck or a balcony splits a cliff or building into a part below eye level (seen at a depression) and a part above (seen at an elevation).

key_terms.definition_md: The horizontal through the observer’s eye, from which angles are measured.

sections.heading: 5. Two right triangles
sections.body_md:
Find the side the two triangles **share**, write one equation from each, and eliminate.

- **Same side** (points $C$, $D$ in line with the foot): distances are **subtracted**. With $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ and gap $g$: $h\sqrt3 - \dfrac{h}{\sqrt3} = g$, so $h = \dfrac{\sqrt3\,g}{2}$; e.g. $g = 40$ gives $h = 20\sqrt3$.
- **Opposite sides:** distances are **added**: $h\sqrt3 + h = 100$ gives $h = 50(\sqrt3 - 1)$.
- **Object on top** (tank on a tower, sign on a pole): the triangles share the base. Tower $12$ m at $45^\circ$, top of tank at $60^\circ$: tank $= 12(\sqrt3 - 1)$.
- **Two buildings:** a horizontal from the top of the shorter one splits the taller into $h$ and $H - h$.

key_terms.definition_md: The side common to both right triangles, usually the height or the base.

visuals.caption: From the foot: $H = 30\tan 60^\circ$. From the top: $H - h = 30\tan 30^\circ$.

sections.heading: 6. Depression from a height; moving objects
sections.body_md:
From the top of a tower of height $h$, objects at depressions $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are $\dfrac{h}{\tan\alpha}$ and $\dfrac{h}{\tan\beta}$ from the foot. The **larger** angle of depression belongs to the **nearer** object. Same side: subtract; opposite sides: add.

**Moving objects:** if an object moves (boat, car, drone) and the angle changes, the distance moved is the difference of the two distances; speed $= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$. A drone at $8$ m/s whose elevation falls from $60^\circ$ to $30^\circ$ in $10$ s flies at $h = 40\sqrt3 \approx 69.28$ m.

Angles do not scale like lengths: halving the distance doubles $\tan\theta$, not $\theta$.

key_terms.definition_md: The one seen at the larger angle of depression.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Figure (1 mark):* correct figure with angles at the observers and right angles marked.
- *Equations (1–2 marks):* a correct ratio equation for each triangle.
- *Solving (1 mark):* elimination and rationalisation.
- *Answer (1 mark):* exact and approximate values with units.

**Common mistakes**
1. Measuring the angle of depression from the vertical, or marking it at the object.
2. Using $\sin$ where height and ground distance call for $\tan$.
3. Ignoring the observer's eye height.
4. Adding distances for points on the same side (or subtracting for opposite sides).
5. Assigning the larger angle of depression to the farther object.
6. Approximating too early; use $\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$ at the end.
7. Assuming angles scale with distances.

questions.stem_md: From the top of a lighthouse, the angle of depression of a boat is $35^\circ$. The angle of elevation of the top of the lighthouse from the boat is
questions.solution_md: The horizontal through the top of the lighthouse is parallel to the sea surface. The line of sight is a transversal, so the angle of depression at the top and the angle of elevation at the boat are **alternate angles**: both $35^\circ$. Option (b) measures the line of sight from the vertical.

questions.stem_md: As an observer walks straight towards a tower, the angle of elevation of its top
questions.solution_md: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}}$. The height is fixed and the distance decreases, so $\tan\theta$ increases, and so does $\theta$.

questions.stem_md: The angle of elevation of an object is the angle between

options.text_md: the line of sight and the ground, when the object is below the eye
the horizontal and the vertical through the object
the line of sight and the horizontal through the eye, when the object is above it
the line of sight and the vertical through the eye

questions.solution_md: Angles of elevation and depression are always measured from the **horizontal** through the observer's eye: elevation when the object is above it, depression when below. Option (a) describes an angle of depression.

questions.stem_md: The angle of elevation of the top of a 30 m tower from a point P on the ground is $45^\circ$. The distance of P from the foot of the tower is
questions.solution_md: $\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{30}{d} = 1$, so $d = 30$ m. At $45^\circ$ the height and the distance are equal.

questions.stem_md: The shadow of a vertical pole is $\sqrt3$ times as long as the pole. The angle of elevation of the sun is
questions.solution_md: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{shadow}} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt3 h} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, so $\theta = 30^\circ$. Option (b) inverts the ratio.

questions.stem_md: A ramp $10$ m long makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the ground. The height of its top above the ground is
questions.solution_md: $\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{h}{10}$, so $h = 10 \times \dfrac12 = 5$ m. Option (c) is the horizontal length ($10\cos 30^\circ$).

questions.stem_md: From the top of a 9 m building, the angle of depression of a scooter parked on the road is $60^\circ$. The distance of the scooter from the building is
questions.solution_md: $\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{9}{d} \Rightarrow d = \dfrac{9}{\sqrt3} = 3\sqrt3 \approx 5.20$ m. Option (d) uses $\tan 30^\circ$ (the angle measured from the vertical).

questions.stem_md: A vertical pole casts a 12 m shadow when the angle of elevation of the sun is $60^\circ$. The height of the pole is
questions.solution_md: $\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{12} \Rightarrow h = 12\sqrt3 \approx 20.78$ m. Option (a) divides by $\sqrt3$ instead of multiplying.

questions.stem_md: When the angle of elevation of the sun rises from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$, the shadow of a 15 m pole becomes shorter by
questions.solution_md: Shadow at $30^\circ$: $\dfrac{15}{\tan 30^\circ} = 15\sqrt3$. At $60^\circ$: $\dfrac{15}{\sqrt3} = 5\sqrt3$. Shorter by $15\sqrt3 - 5\sqrt3 = 10\sqrt3 \approx 17.32$ m. Options (b) and (c) are the two shadows.

questions.stem_md: From a point on the ground 20 m from the foot of a building, the angle of elevation of its top is $60^\circ$. The length of the line of sight from the point to the top is
questions.solution_md: $\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{20}{\text{line of sight}} \Rightarrow$ line of sight $= \dfrac{20}{1/2} = 40$ m. Option (c) is the height of the building.

questions.stem_md: A person whose eyes are 1.5 m above the ground stands 28.5 m from a tower and sees its top at an angle of elevation of $45^\circ$. The height of the tower is
questions.solution_md: Above eye level the tower rises $28.5 \tan 45^\circ = 28.5$ m. Adding the eye height: $28.5 + 1.5 = 30$ m. Option (d) forgets the eye height; option (a) subtracts it.

questions.stem_md: From the top of a 100 m cliff, the angle of depression of a boat is $45^\circ$. The boat is at a distance of
questions.solution_md: $\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{100}{d} = 1$, so $d = 100$ m. Option (c) is the length of the line of sight.

questions.stem_md: The angle of elevation of the top of a 20 m pole from a point on the ground is $30^\circ$. The distance from the point to the top of the pole is
questions.solution_md: $\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{20}{\text{line of sight}}$, so the line of sight is $\dfrac{20}{1/2} = 40$ m. Option (b) is the distance along the ground.

questions.stem_md: A ladder leans against a wall and makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the ground. Its foot is 3.5 m from the wall. The length of the ladder is
questions.solution_md: $\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{3.5}{l} \Rightarrow l = \dfrac{3.5}{1/2} = 7$ m. Option (c) is the height it reaches on the wall.

questions.stem_md: A hot-air balloon at the Pushkar fair is tied to the ground by a straight 200 m cable that makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the ground. The height of the balloon is
questions.solution_md: $\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{200} \Rightarrow h = 200 \times \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = 100\sqrt3 \approx 173.2$ m. Option (d) uses $\cos 60^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: P is on the ground and Q is at the top of a tower. Which statement is always true?

options.text_md: The angle of depression of P from Q is the complement of the angle of elevation of Q from P.
The angle of depression is always larger than the angle of elevation.
The two angles add up to $180^\circ$.
The angle of depression of P from Q equals the angle of elevation of Q from P.

questions.solution_md: The horizontal at $Q$ and the ground at $P$ are parallel, and the line $PQ$ crosses both, so the two angles are alternate angles and are equal.

questions.stem_md: The shadow of a tower is 30 m longer when the sun’s elevation is $30^\circ$ than when it is $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is
questions.solution_md: $h\sqrt3 - \dfrac{h}{\sqrt3} = 30 \Rightarrow \dfrac{3h - h}{\sqrt3} = 30 \Rightarrow h = 15\sqrt3 \approx 25.98$ m.

questions.stem_md: A student whose eyes are 1.6 m above the ground sees the top of a 31.6 m water tower at an angle of elevation of $60^\circ$. Her distance from the tower is
questions.solution_md: Above eye level the tower rises $31.6 - 1.6 = 30$ m. $\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{30}{d} \Rightarrow d = \dfrac{30}{\sqrt3} = 10\sqrt3 \approx 17.32$ m. Option (d) forgets the eye height.

**Reason (R):** The length of the shadow of a pole of height $h$, when the sun’s elevation is $\theta$, is $\dfrac{h}{\tan\theta}$.

**Assertion (A):** From a point 30 m from the foot of a tower, the angle of elevation of its top is $30^\circ$; so the tower is $10\sqrt3$ m tall.

**Reason (R):** In the right triangle formed, the tangent of the angle of elevation equals the height divided by the distance.

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

**Reason (R):** $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}}$.

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: R is true. Halving the distance doubles $\tan\theta$, not $\theta$. Example: a tower seen at $30^\circ$ from $h\sqrt3$; from $\dfrac{h\sqrt3}{2}$, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt3} \approx 1.15$, so $\theta \approx 49^\circ$, not $60^\circ$. A is false.

questions.stem_md: The angle of elevation of an object is measured from the vertical line through the observer.
questions.solution_md: It is measured from the **horizontal** line through the observer's eye.

questions.stem_md: An observer at the top of a tower sees objects on the ground below at angles of depression.
questions.solution_md: The objects are below the horizontal through the observer's eye, so the angles are angles of depression.

questions.stem_md: When the sun’s elevation is $60^\circ$, a 6 m pole casts a shadow $2\sqrt3$ m long.
questions.solution_md: Shadow $= \dfrac{6}{\tan 60^\circ} = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt3} = 2\sqrt3 \approx 3.46$ m.

questions.stem_md: If the top of a tower is seen at $30^\circ$ from a point P, then from a point twice as far away (on the same line) it is seen at $15^\circ$.
questions.solution_md: Doubling the distance halves $\tan\theta$: from $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ to $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt3} \approx 0.29$, an angle of about $16^\circ$, not $15^\circ$. Angles do not scale like distances.

questions.stem_md: An angle of depression can be greater than $90^\circ$.
questions.solution_md: It is the angle between the horizontal and a line of sight below it, so it lies between $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: When the object is above the horizontal through the eye, the angle between the line of sight and that horizontal is called the angle of ___.
questions.solution_md: Above the horizontal: elevation. Below: depression.

questions.stem_md: The top of a 25 m tower is seen from a point P on the ground at an angle of elevation of $45^\circ$. P is ___ m from the foot of the tower.
questions.solution_md: $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, so the distance equals the height: $25$ m.

questions.stem_md: A pole $10\sqrt3$ m high casts a shadow 10 m long. The angle of elevation of the sun is ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{10\sqrt3}{10} = \sqrt3$, so $\theta = 60^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: From the top of a cliff, the angle of depression of a boat is $50^\circ$. From the boat, the angle of elevation of the top of the cliff is ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: Alternate angles between the parallel horizontals: also $50^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A ramp rises 2 m and makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the ground. Its length is ___ m.
questions.solution_md: $\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{2}{l} \Rightarrow l = 4$ m.

questions.stem_md: From a point 40 m from the foot of a tree, the angle of elevation of its top is $30^\circ$. Find the height of the tree in metres, correct to two decimal places. (Use $\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$.)
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{h}{40} \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{40}{\sqrt3} = \dfrac{40\sqrt3}{3}$. **Step 2.** $h \approx \dfrac{40 \times 1.732}{3} = \dfrac{69.28}{3} \approx 23.09$ m.

questions.stem_md: A 15 m ladder leans against a wall, making an angle of $60^\circ$ with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach? Give your answer in metres to two decimal places. (Use $\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$.)
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** $\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{15} \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{15\sqrt3}{2}$. **Step 2.** $h \approx 7.5 \times 1.732 = 12.99$ m.

questions.stem_md: From the top of a 35 m building, the angle of depression of a point on the ground is $45^\circ$. How far is the point from the building (in metres)?
questions.solution_md: $\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{35}{d} = 1$, so $d = 35$ m.

questions.stem_md: Find the length of the shadow of an 8 m pole when the angle of elevation of the sun is $30^\circ$, in metres to two decimal places. (Use $\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$.)
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{8}{s} \Rightarrow s = 8\sqrt3$. **Step 2.** $s \approx 8 \times 1.732 = 13.856 \approx 13.86$ m.

questions.stem_md: From two points 20 m apart on the same side of a tower, and in line with its foot, the angles of elevation of the top are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. Find the height of the tower in metres to two decimal places. (Use $\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$.)
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** Let the height be $h$ and the nearer point be $x$ m from the foot. $\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x} \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt3}$; $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x + 20} \Rightarrow x + 20 = h\sqrt3$. **Step 2.** $h\sqrt3 - \dfrac{h}{\sqrt3} = 20 \Rightarrow \dfrac{2h}{\sqrt3} = 20 \Rightarrow h = 10\sqrt3 \approx 17.32$ m.

questions.stem_md: From the top of a 30 m tower, the angles of depression of two points on opposite sides of the tower, in line with its foot, are $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. Find the distance between the points in metres to two decimal places. (Use $\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$.)
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** At $45^\circ$: distance $= 30$ m. At $60^\circ$: distance $= \dfrac{30}{\sqrt3} = 10\sqrt3$ m. **Step 2.** Total $= 30 + 10\sqrt3 \approx 30 + 17.32 = 47.32$ m.

questions.stem_md: A girl whose eyes are 1.5 m above the ground sees the top of a 21.5 m tree at an angle of elevation of $30^\circ$. How far is she from the tree, in metres to two decimal places? (Use $\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$.)
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** Above eye level the tree rises $21.5 - 1.5 = 20$ m. **Step 2.** $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{20}{d} \Rightarrow d = 20\sqrt3 \approx 20 \times 1.732 = 34.64$ m.

questions.stem_md: A 20 m mobile-phone antenna stands on the roof of a building. From a point on the ground, the angles of elevation of the bottom and the top of the antenna are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. Find the height of the building in metres.

questions.stem_md: From the top of a 40 m tower, a car on a straight road leading to the tower is seen at an angle of depression of $45^\circ$, and a little later at $60^\circ$. How far did the car travel between the two observations?

answer.model_answer_md:
At $45^\circ$ the car is $40$ m from the foot; at $60^\circ$ it is $\dfrac{40}{\sqrt3} = \dfrac{40\sqrt3}{3}$ m.

questions.stem_md: The shadow of a vertical tower becomes 10 m shorter when the sun’s elevation rises from $45^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. Find the height of the tower.

answer.model_answer_md:
At $45^\circ$ the shadow equals the height $h$; at $60^\circ$ it is $\dfrac{h}{\sqrt3}$.

$h - \dfrac{h}{\sqrt3} = 10 \Rightarrow h\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3 - 1}{\sqrt3}\right) = 10 \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{10\sqrt3}{\sqrt3 - 1}$.

Rationalising: $h = \dfrac{10\sqrt3(\sqrt3 + 1)}{2} = 5(3 + \sqrt3) = 15 + 5\sqrt3 \approx 23.66$ m.

questions.solution_md: **Check:** the shadows are $23.66$ m and $\dfrac{23.66}{1.732} \approx 13.66$ m, which differ by $10$ m.

questions.stem_md: A 4 m signboard is fixed on top of a vertical pole. From a point P on the ground, the angles of elevation of the bottom and the top of the signboard are $30^\circ$ and $45^\circ$. Find the height of the pole.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let the pole be $h$ m and P be $d$ m from it. $\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{h + 4}{d} \Rightarrow d = h + 4$; $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{h}{d} \Rightarrow d = h\sqrt3$.

$h\sqrt3 = h + 4 \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt3 - 1} = \dfrac{4(\sqrt3 + 1)}{2} = 2(\sqrt3 + 1) \approx 5.46$ m.

questions.solution_md: P is then $h + 4 \approx 9.46$ m from the pole.

answer.model_answer_md:
The horizontal from the top of the shorter building meets the taller one 20 m above the ground. Above that level, the taller building rises $50\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{50}{\sqrt3} = \dfrac{50\sqrt3}{3} \approx 28.87$ m.

Height $= 20 + \dfrac{50\sqrt3}{3} \approx 48.87$ m.

questions.solution_md: Split the taller building at the level of the shorter one.

questions.stem_md: Arjun claims: "When the sun’s elevation falls from $60^\circ$ to $30^\circ$, the shadow of a pole doubles in length." Test his claim for a 9 m pole.

answer.model_answer_md:
At $60^\circ$: shadow $= \dfrac{9}{\sqrt3} = 3\sqrt3 \approx 5.20$ m. At $30^\circ$: shadow $= 9\sqrt3 \approx 15.59$ m.

questions.stem_md: A boat sails straight towards a 50 m lighthouse. The angle of depression of the boat from the top changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ in 2 minutes. Find the speed of the boat in metres per minute.

answer.model_answer_md:
Distances from the foot: $50\sqrt3$ (at $30^\circ$) and $\dfrac{50}{\sqrt3}$ (at $60^\circ$).

Distance sailed $= 50\sqrt3 - \dfrac{50}{\sqrt3} = \dfrac{150 - 50}{\sqrt3} = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt3} \approx 57.74$ m.

Speed $= \dfrac{57.74}{2} \approx 28.87$ m per minute.

questions.solution_md: Distance first, then divide by time.

questions.stem_md:
Building P is 20 m tall. From the foot of P, the angle of elevation of the top of a taller building Q is $60^\circ$; from the top of P, the angle of elevation of the top of Q is $45^\circ$.

(a) Draw a labelled figure.

(b) Find the distance between the buildings.

(c) Find the height of Q.

(d) Find how much taller Q is than P.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Figure: verticals $P$ ($20$ m) and $Q$ ($H$ m), $d$ m apart; from the foot of $P$ a line to the top of $Q$ at $60^\circ$; from the top of $P$ a dashed horizontal and a line to the top of $Q$ at $45^\circ$.

(b) From the foot: $H = d\tan 60^\circ = d\sqrt3$. From the top: $H - 20 = d\tan 45^\circ = d$. So $d\sqrt3 - d = 20 \Rightarrow d = \dfrac{20}{\sqrt3 - 1} = 10(\sqrt3 + 1) \approx 27.32$ m.

(c) $H = d\sqrt3 = 10(3 + \sqrt3) \approx 47.32$ m.

(d) $H - 20 = d \approx 27.32$ m.

questions.solution_md: Rationalise: $\dfrac{20}{\sqrt3 - 1} \times \dfrac{\sqrt3 + 1}{\sqrt3 + 1} = \dfrac{20(\sqrt3 + 1)}{2}$.

questions.stem_md:
A hot-air balloon at the Pushkar fair rises vertically from a point O on the ground. Seema watches from a point S on level ground, 100 m from O. The angle of elevation of the balloon changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ in 2 minutes.

(a) Find the heights of the balloon at the two moments.

(b) How far did it rise?

(c) Find its average speed of rising in metres per minute.

(d) Find the distance of the balloon from Seema at the second moment.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $h_1 = 100\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt3} \approx 57.74$ m; $h_2 = 100\tan 60^\circ = 100\sqrt3 \approx 173.21$ m.

(b) Rise $= 100\sqrt3 - \dfrac{100}{\sqrt3} = \dfrac{200}{\sqrt3} \approx 115.47$ m.

(c) Speed $= \dfrac{115.47}{2} \approx 57.74$ m per minute.

(d) Distance from Seema $= \dfrac{100}{\cos 60^\circ} = 200$ m.

questions.solution_md: The rise is exactly twice the first height, since $100\sqrt3 = 3 \times \dfrac{100}{\sqrt3}$.

questions.stem_md:
From a point P on level ground, the angle of elevation of the top T of a vertical tower is $60^\circ$. From a window Q, 20 m vertically above P, the angle of elevation of T is $30^\circ$.

(a) Draw a labelled figure.

(b) Find the horizontal distance between P and the tower.

(c) Find the height of the tower.

(d) Find QT, and show that triangle PQT is isosceles.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Figure: $P$ on the ground, $Q$ 20 m above $P$, tower $BT$ at distance $d$; from $P$ the line $PT$ at $60^\circ$ to the ground; from $Q$ a dashed horizontal meeting $BT$ at $M$ (20 m up) and $QT$ at $30^\circ$ to it.

(b) From $P$: $H = d\sqrt3$. From $Q$: $H - 20 = \dfrac{d}{\sqrt3}$. Subtracting: $d\sqrt3 - \dfrac{d}{\sqrt3} = 20 \Rightarrow \dfrac{2d}{\sqrt3} = 20 \Rightarrow d = 10\sqrt3 \approx 17.32$ m.

(c) $H = 10\sqrt3 \times \sqrt3 = 30$ m.

(d) $QT = \dfrac{d}{\cos 30^\circ} = \dfrac{10\sqrt3}{\sqrt3/2} = 20$ m $= PQ$. So triangle $PQT$ is isosceles with $PQ = QT = 20$ m. (Also $\angle QPT = 90^\circ - 60^\circ = 30^\circ$ and $\angle QTP = 60^\circ - 30^\circ = 30^\circ$: equal base angles.)

questions.solution_md: **Check:** $PT = \dfrac{d}{\cos 60^\circ} = 20\sqrt3$, and the isosceles triangle with sides $20, 20, 20\sqrt3$ has apex angle $120^\circ$ at $Q$.

questions.stem_md:
A 12 m vertical pole stands on level ground in Jaipur.

(a) Find the length of its shadow when the sun’s elevation is $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$.

(b) By how much does the shadow shorten as the elevation rises from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$?

(c) At what elevation is the shadow as long as the pole?

(d) Can the shadow ever be shorter than half the pole while the sun’s elevation is at most $60^\circ$? Justify.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Shadow $= \dfrac{12}{\tan\theta}$: at $30^\circ$, $12\sqrt3 \approx 20.78$ m; at $45^\circ$, $12$ m; at $60^\circ$, $\dfrac{12}{\sqrt3} = 4\sqrt3 \approx 6.93$ m.

(b) $12\sqrt3 - 4\sqrt3 = 8\sqrt3 \approx 13.86$ m.

(c) Shadow $=$ pole when $\tan\theta = 1$, i.e. at $45^\circ$.

(d) The shadow is shortest when the elevation is largest. At $60^\circ$ it is $4\sqrt3 \approx 6.93$ m, which is more than half the pole ($6$ m). So for elevations up to $60^\circ$ the shadow is never shorter than half the pole.

questions.solution_md: For the shadow to be $6$ m we would need $\tan\theta = 2$, an elevation above $60^\circ$ (since $\tan 60^\circ \approx 1.73 < 2$).

questions.stem_md:
A vertical flagpole stands on level ground.

(a) Draw a labelled figure for part (b).

(b) From a point $A$, $20$ m from the foot of the flagpole, the angle of elevation of its top is $45^\circ$. Find the height of the flagpole.

(c) How far from the foot must an observer stand for the angle of elevation of the top to be $60^\circ$?

(d) How far from the foot must an observer stand for the angle of elevation of the top to be $30^\circ$?

(e) Find the length of the line of sight from $A$ to the top of the flagpole.

(Use $\sqrt2 \approx 1.414$ and $\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Figure: flagpole $PF$ with foot $F$ on the ground, point $A$ on the ground $20$ m from $F$, line of sight $AP$, angle $PAF = 45^\circ$, right angle at $F$.

(b) $\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{PF}{AF}$, so $PF = 20 \times 1 = 20$ m.

(c) $\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{20}{d}$, so $d = \dfrac{20}{\sqrt3} = \dfrac{20\sqrt3}{3} \approx 11.55$ m.

(d) $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{20}{d}$, so $d = 20\sqrt3 \approx 34.64$ m.

(e) $\cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{AF}{AP}$, so $AP = \dfrac{20}{1/\sqrt2} = 20\sqrt2 \approx 28.28$ m.

questions.solution_md: Each part is one right triangle with the flagpole as the opposite side; $\tan$ links height and ground distance, $\cos$ gives the line of sight.
